title: Inside the SEC's 24-Hour Trading Roundtable: Nasdaq's Chuck Mack on Building a Resilient Overnight Market
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: The Nasdaq Stock Market will introduce a new session running from 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. ET, to create “23/5” trading: 23 hours of continuous markets, five days a week, with a one-hour pause each night for processing and trade-date rollover.
content: On December 6, U.S. equities markets will take their biggest step yet toward an always-on market. The Nasdaq Stock Market will introduce a new session running from 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. ET, to create “23/5” trading: 23 hours of continuous markets, five days a week, with a one-hour pause each night for processing and trade-date rollover. The move to 23/5 trading was the backdrop for the SEC Roundtable on Preparations for 24-Hour Trading in Washington, where regulators, exchanges, clearing agencies, market makers, and brokers gathered to stress-test one question above all others: Is the market actually ready? For Chuck Mack, Senior Vice President of North American Markets at Nasdaq, as well as nearly all of his fellow panelists, the answer was a confident yes — the product of a multi-year, industrywide effort rather than a single-threaded leap. "There are a lot of green lights," Mack told the panel. "We are on track across both of our roles as processor of the Tape C SIP [Securities Information Processor] and as an operating exchange. [We have] a lot of confidence in the December 6 date — none of us see it as a target, we see it as the go-live.” A Deliberate Approach Mack was transparent that Nasdaq was careful in its approach to 23/5 trading. "We listened to the market and to our clients, then we got very involved,” he said, citing input from the APAC region, from U.S. clients, and from infrastructure providers. That feedback loop shaped the structure of the new trading day itself, including the 8:00–9:00 p.m. ET pause built in ahead of the overnight session. Mack credited the collaborative process behind the SIP's national market system plans, which coordinate the consolidated tape across exchanges. “It can be slow and challenging" to move something forward by committee, he acknowledged — but "the industry really came together in a very good way." Resiliency as a "Puzzle Piece” Speaking about how firms like Nasdaq are building resiliency into their 23/5 plans, Mack stepped back to make a broader point about how the industry approaches complexity. "We all operate — together and separately — multiple technological systems," he said. "Across the entire industry I wouldn't know how to count them all, and even within firms there are many interdependent systems.” Rather than treating 23/5 as an isolated challenge, Mack argued it fits into a discipline the industry has already mastered: designing elements as pieces interacting with a broader puzzle. “You don't design systems without thinking about interdependencies — how you maintain the system, do failover, do software updates, and add new products and features,” he said, adding that 23/5 trading "is just another thing that you're pulling into that complex but well-designed system across the entire industry.” That same instinct to treat resilience as an evolving discipline carried into the panel's discussion of cybersecurity. Asked how AI-accelerated cyber threats might change the calculus for an overnight session, Mack noted that Nasdaq already runs a wide array of systems around the clock. "The fact that we'll have a couple more systems running eight hours longer doesn't significantly change the cyber policies and standards we set. We have a very robust program that constantly evolves as new technology emerges, and we account for that.” A Good First Step, Not a Finished Product As the industry continues to gear up for December 6, Nasdaq’s perspective continues to be clear: the move to 23/5 trading represents a deliberate, phased expansion of market access — built on proven implementation discipline, tested collaboration across the industry, and a clear-eyed view that resilience is never finished, only continuously reinforced. Reflecting on the SEC Roundtable, Mack said, “These industry conversations provide such a valuable opportunity for collaboration and information sharing. As we approach December 6th, Nasdaq’s guiding principles are focused on transparent communication, industry cohesion, and focusing on client needs – that’s what will make this launch a success.”

title: Nasdaq Launches Economic Opportunity Index to Help Investors Measure Readiness for Innovation-Led Growth
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: The Economic Opportunity Index, a new data-driven framework from the Nasdaq Economic Institute and Oxford Economics, covers 123 economies across five core pillars.
content: Investors and market watchers are always eager for a holistic view of the innovation-led growth taking place in the economies around the world. A new data-driven framework from the Nasdaq Economic Institute and Oxford Economics, the Economic Opportunity Index (EOI) will now be a valuable resource for them. Launching today, the Economic Opportunity Index, covers 123 economies across five core pillars: Innovation Engine, Economic Governance and Predictability, Capital Dynamism, Market Strength and Resilience, and Talent and Opportunity. It draws on a combination of proprietary Nasdaq data and publicly available sources, with historical data extending back to 2000. The Nasdaq Newsroom spoke with Michael Normyle, U.S. Economist at the Nasdaq Economic Institute, about the Index's design, its relationship to GDP, and what stood out in the research. What is the Economic Opportunity Index? The Economic Opportunity Index is a quarterly index that assesses whether the structural ingredients supporting innovation-led, resilient growth are present and working together in a given economy. Rather than predicting which economies will outperform, the index evaluates their readiness to do so including the structural conditions that support long-term economic resilience, competitiveness, and innovation-led growth in our white paper with Oxford Economics. Most economic indicators tell us where an economy is; the EOI helps reveal where it's headed by evaluating the five pillars that determine whether the conditions for durable, resilient growth are in place. How does the EOI differ from traditional economic indices? GDP remains the standard measure of a country's economic performance, but it only captures output. The EOI isn't trying to replace GDP; it's a complement to it. While GDP measures output alone, the EOI takes a more holistic view that incorporates demographics, market inputs, among others within the Index's five pillars. What does the EOI measure? The index is built around five core pillars: Innovation Engine, Economic Governance and Predictability, Capital Dynamism, Market Strength and Resilience and Talent and Opportunity. Those pillars are meant to capture longstanding measures of an economy, like governance and political stability, alongside newer additions like artificial intelligence readiness. It uses those five pillars to assess an economy’s readiness for innovation-led growth. How is the EOI structured methodologically? The index is organized in three tiers: individual indicators, sub-pillars, and pillars. There are 44 individual indicators, which are grouped into sub-pillars, which then combine into the five top pillars. Those five pillars are then aggregated into a total EOI score. Scores are calibrated on a scale centered at 100 and indexed to the fourth quarter of 2025. This framework makes the scores comparable across countries and over time. A score above 100 reflects above-average performance relative to that period, while a score below 100 reflects below-average performance. Who is the EOI designed for? It's a fairly broad group. Policymakers can use the EOI to make informed decisions, since it works as a measure of readiness and can show areas of strength and potential improvement. Corporates that need to make investment decisions can use it too, to quickly narrow down a group of economies that match their needs and focus on whichever pillars are most relevant to their particular investment at the moment. It should also prove to be a useful tool for researchers, which can uncover new findings from the EOI. How often will the EOI be updated, and where will findings be published? The EOI will be published quarterly on Nasdaq.com. This will offer users a relatively current view on how an economy is trending.The quarterly cadence is relatively unusual for broad measures of economic activity, which tend to be lagged, sometimes reflecting past data. Did your research turn up any noteworthy patterns? Looking across lower-income, middle-income, and higher-income countries, different pillars stood out as most significant at different stages. For lower-income countries, capital dynamism and talent and opportunity were the most statistically significant pillars. The innovation engine pillar became more important for upper-middle and high-income nations. And for high-income countries specifically, talent and opportunity reemerged as a key factor. That may reflect brain-drain dynamics, since high-income countries can both lose people to other economies and gain people from them. Separately, the research found that the Economic Governance and Predictability pillar showed close to a 10-year lead over real GDP per capita performance. That's consistent with both the existing literature and what we heard from experts in the field: Economic Governance and Predictability are essentially a prerequisite for long-term growth. Explore the index and read the joint white paper.

title: Building Connections, Empowering Growth: Romana Maione’s WIN Leadership Journey
author: Hannah Goodfriend
description: As a leader within Women in Nasdaq (WIN), Romana Maione is helping create meaningful opportunities for connection, mentorship, and professional growth across the organization. Through her roles supporting global partnerships and Lean In Circles, she brings a collaborative, people-centered approach to fostering inclusive spaces where employees can share experiences, build confidence, and strengthen their sense of belonging at Nasdaq.
content: As a leader within Women in Nasdaq (WIN), Romana Maione is helping create meaningful opportunities for connection, mentorship, and professional growth across the organization. Through her roles supporting global partnerships and Lean In Circles, she brings a collaborative, people-centered approach to fostering inclusive spaces where employees can share experiences, build confidence, and strengthen their sense of belonging at Nasdaq. 1. What leadership position have you taken on in your Employee Network, and what do you do in this role? (Answer is required for this question.) In the Co-Lead of WIN Global Partnerships role, I help create opportunities for networking, mentorship, and professional development, while fostering meaningful connections and open dialogue among employees across the organization. I collaborate closely with the Purpose team and coordinate events to raise awareness on sensitive issues, upskill colleagues, or boost networking. 2. In your own words, what is the mission of your Employee Network? The mission of Women in Nasdaq is to create a supportive and inclusive community focused on gender equality that helps employees grow professionally, build meaningful relationships, and learn from one another. It provides opportunities to share experiences, expand perspectives, and empower individuals to reach their full potential. 3. How has being an Employee Network Leader contributed to your professional development at Nasdaq? Being an Employee Network Leader has strengthened my ability to influence without authority, engage diverse groups of people, and build relationships across functions and geographies. It has also provided opportunities to practice leadership in a different context while contributing to a cause I care deeply about. 4. What skills have you gained or improved since taking on an Employee Network leadership role? I have further developed skills in communication, facilitation, stakeholder engagement, event planning, and community building. Most importantly, I have learned how to create environments where people feel comfortable sharing ideas, challenges, and experiences. 5. How has being in an Employee Network leadership role contributed to your sense of community at Nasdaq? It has significantly expanded my network and strengthened my connection to colleagues across the company. Through WIN and Lean In Circles, I have been able to build relationships with employees I may never have met through my day-to-day work, creating a stronger sense of belonging and community. 6. What does “integrity” mean to you as an Employee Network Leader? Integrity means creating an environment built on trust, respect, and authenticity. It means listening to diverse perspectives, treating everyone fairly, and ensuring that all voices feel heard and valued. 7. What have you learned about leading a team or managing others in your role as an Employee Network Leader? I have learned that effective leadership is often less about directing people and more about creating an environment where they feel empowered to contribute. Employee Networks rely on influence, collaboration, and shared purpose rather than formal reporting structures, which has reinforced the importance of listening, building consensus, and recognizing the unique strengths that each person brings to the team. 8. How have Employee Networks enabled you to honor your culture, heritage or background at work? As someone who was born and raised in Italy and has lived and worked in several countries before joining Nasdaq in New York, Employee Networks have provided opportunities to share experiences, perspectives, and insights shaped by a multicultural background. They create spaces where employees can bring their authentic selves to work, celebrate different cultures, and learn from one another, which helps foster a more inclusive and globally connected workplace. 9. What has been the most rewarding moment as an Employee Network leader? The most rewarding moments are seeing meaningful connections form between colleagues and hearing how participation in a WIN event, mentorship opportunity, or Lean In Circle discussion positively impacted someone's confidence, career development, or sense of belonging at Nasdaq. 10. How do Employee Networks contribute to in-office culture at Nasdaq? Employee Networks help create a more connected, inclusive, and engaging workplace. They bring people together across teams and backgrounds, encourage collaboration, and provide opportunities for learning and relationship-building that strengthen our culture both in and out of the office. 11. What have you learned about your own or other cultures or communities as an Employee Network leader? One of the most valuable lessons has been recognizing how much we can learn from hearing different experiences and perspectives. Employee Networks create spaces where people can share their unique backgrounds and stories, which helps build understanding, empathy, and stronger connections across the organization.

title: Leading with Purpose: Jesse Calixte on Community, Sustainability and the Power of Connection
author: Hannah Goodfriend
description: As the Green Team Chapter Lead in Atlanta, Jesse Calixte has found meaningful ways to connect his personal values with his work at Nasdaq. Through volunteer events, community partnerships and sustainability-focused initiatives, Jesse helps create opportunities for colleagues to step outside their day-to-day roles, build stronger relationships and make a positive impact together. In this interview, he shares how Employee Network leadership has shaped his view of purpose-driven leadership, workplace culture and the importance of creating experiences people genuinely want to be part of.
content: As the Green Team Chapter Lead in Atlanta, Jesse Calixte has found meaningful ways to connect his personal values with his work at Nasdaq. Through volunteer events, community partnerships and sustainability-focused initiatives, Jesse helps create opportunities for colleagues to step outside their day-to-day roles, build stronger relationships and make a positive impact together. In this interview, he shares how Employee Network leadership has shaped his view of purpose-driven leadership, workplace culture and the importance of creating experiences people genuinely want to be part of. 1. What leadership position have you taken on in your Employee Network, and what do you do in this role? I lead the Green Team in Atlanta. My day job is very different. I spend a lot of time working with contracts, numbers, and details where being precise matters. With the Green Team, I get to think much more about the environment, people, ideas, and how to turn an idea into something people actually want to be part of. A big part of my role is organizing events, but that is only part of it. The harder part is getting people to give up a few hours of their day for something they are not required to do. Everyone is busy. So when someone decides to spend an afternoon helping clean up a park or volunteering in the community, I want them to feel like it was worth their time. That is what I try to create with the Green Team. Not just events, but experiences people remember. 2. How has being an Employee Network Leader contributed to your professional development at Nasdaq? My background is in contracts, finance, and accounting, where success is often measured by accuracy, attention to detail, and getting to the right answer. Being a Green Team leader has helped me develop a very different skill set. It has taught me how to bring people together around an idea, even when I don't have authority or a formal role in managing them. I've learned that leadership is not always about authority. Most of the people who participate in Green Team activities don't report to me and don't have to be there. If they're giving their time, it's because they believe in the idea and feel connected to the purpose behind it. That has taught me how to communicate more effectively, build trust, and create momentum through collaboration. What makes the experience especially rewarding is seeing people choose to get involved because they genuinely care and want to make a difference. Those experiences have helped me grow as a leader and complement the skills I use every day in my role at Nasdaq. 3. What does “integrity” mean to you as an Employee Network Leader? Integrity is simple to me. If I say I am going to do something, I should do it. So for me, integrity is not about having the right answer in a meeting or saying the right thing when people are watching. It is what you do afterward. If I tell people we are going to do something, I want them to know they can trust me to see it through, even when there is no spotlight on it. 4. What have you learned about leading a team or managing others in your role as an Employee Network Leader? I learned that you cannot make people care. When we partnered with the City of Sandy Springs to clean up the Big Trees Forest Preserve park for Earth Month this year, nobody on the team worked for me. I could not tell them they had to be there. They showed up because they believed it was worth their time and because they care about the community. That changed the way I think about leadership. People don't get involved simply because of a title. They get involved when they understand and connect with the purpose behind something. As a network leader, I've found that my role is less about leading and more about helping others see the "why" and creating space for them to be part of it. 5. How have Employee Networks enabled you to honor your culture, heritage or background at work? For me, community has always been important. I have always believed that where you work should be more than a place you show up, do your job, and leave. The people around you matter, and the environment you help create matters. The Green Team has given me a way to bring that mindset into my work. It has allowed me to contribute to something outside of my normal responsibilities while creating opportunities for other people to get involved too. I think that is one of the things I value most about the experience. It allows me to bring a part of who I am to work and connect my professional life with values that matter to me personally. 6. What has been the most rewarding moment as an Employee Network leader? The cleanup at the John Ripley Forbes Big Trees Forest Preserve in Sandy Springs stands out to me. We partnered with the City of Sandy Springs for Earth Month and spent the day working alongside other Green Team members to care for a place that people in the community use. What made it rewarding wasn't just the work itself. It was seeing colleagues choose to spend their time giving back together. It reminded me how much impact a small group of committed people can have. 7. How do Employee Networks contribute to in-office culture at Nasdaq? I think culture is built in the moments that are not on your calendar. You can work with someone for months and only know them through Teams meetings, emails, and projects. Then you spend an afternoon volunteering together and suddenly you know something about them that you would never have learned in a meeting. That is what Employee Networks can create. The Green Team gives people a reason to step away from their normal responsibilities and do something together. Those connections matter. They make the workplace feel more human. I also like that Employee Networks give employees a chance to be part of the culture instead of just talking about it. We all have a role in deciding what kind of place Nasdaq becomes. For me, the Green Team is one small way I can contribute to that.

title: The Night Shift You Never See: How AI Agents Are Changing Capital Markets Operations
author: Sophie Marnhier-Foy
description: Learn governed AI agents could help capital markets teams investigate issues, prioritize work and act more efficiently without compromising control - and how Nasdaq Calypso plans to support agents in the platform.
content: Picture the start of your day: You pour a coffee, sit down and open your screen. Before you begin, AI agents have already completed defined overnight work within established workflows. Reconciliation breaks have been analyzed, settlements at risk of failing have been flagged and exceptions have been prioritized for review. The work has not been taken out of your hands. Instead, the analysis and preparation are ready, allowing you to begin with the issues that need your judgment rather than the steps required to find them. Your priorities are clear. This is becoming possible for capital markets operations through advances in AI and agentic workflows. AI agents represent a new source of intelligent capacity. More than another tool or dashboard, they can carry out defined work when called by a person, workflow, schedule or event, helping teams across front, middle and back offices focus their time on judgment, priorities and strategy. How close are we to this new reality? We announced our first capability, available today, which helps users investigate and interpret information within established workflows. From that starting point, Nasdaq Calypso plans to support the future development of governed AI agents that could help users work more efficiently and effectively over time, within established workflows and controls. Myth, Reality or Just a Better Chatbot?

title: Advancing Capital Markets Reform, Digital Assets and Financial Crime Prevention at Eurofi Dublin 2026
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Policymakers, regulators, and financial industry leaders converged in Dublin earlier this month for the 2026 Eurofi Financial Forum.
content: Image Policymakers, regulators, and financial industry leaders converged in Dublin earlier this month for the 2026 Eurofi Financial Forum, held in association with the Irish EU Council Presidency on the eve of the informal Ecofin meeting. Twice a year, Eurofi brings together senior leaders from the public and private sectors to shape the conversation on Europe's financial, regulatory, economic, and technological future. A Nasdaq delegation led by Nikolaj Kosakewitsch, Head of European Market Services; Roland Chai, Head of Digital Liquidity Networks; and Kamlesh Harry, Principal Strategic Advisor at Nasdaq Verafin, joined policymakers, regulators, and industry stakeholders from across Europe and beyond for three days of discussion spanning capital markets competitiveness, the Savings and Investments Union (SIU), tokenization and digital assets, artificial intelligence, and the fight against financial crime. Driving the conversation on market structure reform Kosakewitsch joined the panel "Securities Trading: Fragmentation, Future Trends and MISP Implications," where participants examined how the proposed Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP) could reduce fragmentation, improve liquidity, and strengthen the efficiency of European capital markets. "There is a real opportunity to make European capital markets more efficient, competitive, and attractive through effective implementation of MISP," said Kosakewitsch. "The conversations in Dublin reflected a growing determination across both the public and private sectors to move from discussion to delivery and strengthen Europe's position in global capital markets." That sense of momentum carried through the full three days, with broad support emerging across sectors for reforms that could help build a more integrated, globally competitive European marketplace. Rethinking capital markets through tokenization Chai brought Nasdaq's perspective on digital assets to the forum, highlighting how tokenization could reshape the foundations of European market infrastructure. "The opportunity with tokenization is not simply to digitize existing processes, but to rethink how capital markets operate," said Chai. "By reducing friction, improving transparency, and streamlining post-trade activities, tokenization can help address some of the long-standing structural challenges facing European markets. Combined with broader integration efforts such as the SIU, it has the potential to make Europe's capital markets more efficient, accessible, and competitive on a global scale." Confronting AI-enabled financial crime On the payments and financial crime front, Harry spoke on the panel "Retail Payment Innovation in the AI Era," where discussions explored how financial institutions are pairing AI, behavioral intelligence, and advanced analytics to strengthen fraud detection, even as criminal networks use the same technologies to operate with greater speed and sophistication. "As criminals become more sophisticated and operate across borders, collaboration is no longer optional," said Harry. "Financial institutions, regulators, law enforcement, technology providers, and payment networks all have a role to play. Trusted data sharing and collective action will be essential if we are to stay ahead of increasingly complex financial crime threats." Participants throughout the forum voiced strong support for greater cross-border collaboration and trusted data sharing, with particular optimism around the EU's new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) and its potential to deliver a more coordinated, pan-European approach to combating financial crime. Looking ahead Speakers across panels agreed that Europe's financial sector is looking for integration, simplification, and stronger cross-border collaboration to remain competitive on the global stage. Nasdaq leaders also contributed two articles to the biannual Eurofi Views Magazine: Kosakewitsch on strengthening EU market structure for more competitive and integrated capital markets, and Stephanie Champion, Head of Nasdaq Verafin, on protecting Europe's financial system in the age of AI-enabled threats.

title: Do I Still Need Bonds or Gold in My Portfolio Today?
author: Yinan Xiao
description: Bonds or gold: which offers stronger diversification today? Nasdaq Index Research examines 30 years of data to assess how each asset has supported portfolio diversification, risk reduction, returns, and recovery through different market cycles and periods of stress.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Bonds generally provided stronger diversification, while gold offered more consistent benefits across market regimes. Combining bonds and gold delivered greater diversification than relying on either asset alone. Gold maintained a low correlation with equities, while bond-equity correlations increased after 2021. Equity/gold portfolios historically delivered higher median returns and fewer extreme negative outcomes over longer holding periods. Both bonds and gold improved portfolio resilience, but gold provided stronger protection during the Inflation Shock. For decades, bonds have played a unique role alongside equities in diversified portfolios. They not only provided a source of income but also often helped offset equity market weakness. This was particularly evident during periods of economic slowdown or market stress, when stocks and bonds tended to move in opposite directions. However, this relationship has not always held. In 2022, for example, rising inflation and higher interest rates caused both stocks and bonds to decline at the same time. As a result, many investors began to question whether bonds could still provide the same diversification benefits they once did. This also raises a related question about the role gold can play alongside bonds in diversifying equity exposure. This blog examines the role of bonds and gold in portfolio diversification. We compare how consistently they have provided diversification across market regimes, which asset mixes delivered the strongest historical diversification within the historical sample and methodology described, and how each contributed to portfolio returns and downside protection. Diversification starts with how assets move together To assess whether two assets can help diversify one another, investors often look at correlation. Correlation measures how closely the returns of two assets move together. When correlation is high, the assets tend to rise and fall at the same time, providing limited diversification benefits. When correlation is low or negative, the assets tend to behave differently, helping reduce the overall volatility of a portfolio. Chart 1: Bond-equity correlation increased after 2021, while gold remained weakly correlated with equities. Image Historical data show that the relationship between U.S. bonds and U.S. equities has evolved across different economic regimes. As shown in Chart 1, the equity-bond correlation (blue line) was generally positive before 2001. From 2001 to 2020, the correlation was predominantly negative, allowing bonds to serve not only as a diversifier but also as an effective hedge against equity market weakness. Since 2021, however, the negative correlation has largely disappeared, with the relationship fluctuating between near-zero and positive levels. This shift reflects more frequent periods of simultaneous declines in bonds and equities, compared with much of the previous two decades. One possible explanation is that elevated inflation and rising interest rate expectations increasingly influenced both asset classes. Has gold exhibited a similar pattern? Examining the correlation between U.S. equities and gold suggests otherwise. Unlike bonds, gold has generally maintained a low correlation with U.S. equities (purple line) since 2001, with the correlation fluctuating around zero. This suggests that gold has generally behaved differently from U.S. equities, supporting its potential role as a diversifier. However, correlation alone does not tell us how much portfolio risk is reduced. To assess this effect in greater detail, we next examine the Diversification Ratio. Measuring diversification using the Diversification Ratio (DR) The Diversification Ratio quantifies the extent to which portfolio risk is reduced by combining different assets. It is defined as the weighted volatility of the portfolio's constituent assets divided by the volatility of the overall portfolio: Image The lowest possible value of the DR is 1, which occurs when there is no diversification benefit and the portfolio volatility equals the weighted average volatility of its constituent assets. Higher values indicate greater diversification benefits, as portfolio volatility is lower relative to the weighted average volatility of its individual holdings. Chart 2 compares the DR of two simple portfolios: 50% U.S. equity / 50% U.S. bond and 50% U.S. equity / 50% gold. Overall, diversification benefits varied over time with two observations worth noting. First, the equity/gold portfolio rarely recorded a higher DR than the equity/bond portfolio over the sample period, indicating greater diversification benefits from bonds under the selected inputs and methodology. Second, the equity/bond portfolio exhibited much greater variation in diversification benefits than the equity/gold portfolio. This was most apparent during the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the subsequent recovery period, coinciding with the strong negative equity-bond correlation observed during this period, as shown in Chart 1 . Chart 2: Bonds' diversification swings over time; gold's holds steadier Image Using 30 years of historical data, we calculate the DR across a range of equity, bond, and gold allocations and identify the allocation that maximizes DR. Chart 3 shows how DR varies with equity exposure, with the remaining portfolio weight allocated to bonds, gold, or a combination of both. When equity allocations exceed 65% (left of the dashed line), changes in the bond-gold mix have little impact on DR, as equities remain the dominant source of portfolio risk. As equity exposure falls below 65% (right of the dashed line), differences across bond-gold allocations become more pronounced. DR rises as equity exposure declines, reaches a peak, and then gradually falls, suggesting that the strongest diversification benefits come from a balanced mix of assets rather than an extreme allocation. Portfolios combining bonds and gold (purple, navy, and tan lines) generally exhibit higher DRs than portfolios invested solely in bonds or gold (dark blue and gold lines), indicating that the two assets provide complementary sources of diversification. Among the portfolios tested, the highest DR was achieved with an allocation of 25% equities, 37.5% bonds, and 37.5% gold over the 30-year sample period. Chart 3: Diversification benefits become more pronounced below 65% equity exposure Image Building on the previous analysis, we examine whether the portfolio with the highest DR over the full sample period remains the most effective diversifier across different market regimes. For simplicity, we focus on portfolios where, after setting the equity allocation, the remaining weight is evenly split between bonds and gold. Chart 4 plots equity weight on the x-axis and DR on the y-axis, with each of the five lines representing a different market regime. Three observations stand out: First, the GFC and Recovery period (green line) delivered a higher DR than the other regimes across almost all asset mixes, consistent with the strongly negative equity-bond correlation observed in Chart 1. By contrast, the Tech Boom and Bust period (blue line) records the lowest DR until equity exposure falls below approximately 35%. Second, the shapes of the lines provide further insight into how the DR-maximizing allocation has shifted across regimes. DR continues to rise through the lowest equity allocation tested during the Tech Boom and Bust (blue line) and Global Expansion (orange line), while the GFC and Recovery period (green line), Low-Rate Environment (purple line), and Inflationary Reset (yellow line) peak at around 30% equity before declining. Third, among these peaks, the GFC and Recovery period reaches the highest DR, at approximately 1.90, while the Inflationary Reset records the lowest, at approximately 1.54. The weaker diversification during the recent regime is consistent with the renewed positive correlation between equities and bonds shown in Chart 1, returning to the question raised at the beginning of this analysis about whether bonds still provide the same diversification benefits investors once relied on. Overall, the shape of the diversification curve and the level of diversification achieved vary across market regimes. Despite these differences, the DR-maximizing portfolio remains consistently diversified across regimes, with peak diversification typically attained at equity allocations of around 20% to 30%. Chart 4: Peak DR was strongest during the GFC & Recovery and weakest during the Inflationary Reset. Image Beyond the DR: return shape and crisis resilience Beyond the DR, portfolio return characteristics provide additional insight into the roles played by bonds and gold. Chart 5 compares the distribution of rolling annualized returns over the past 30 years for three holding horizons: 1 year, 5 years, and 10 years for two portfolios: a 50% U.S. equity / 50% U.S. bond portfolio and a 50% U.S. equity / 50% gold portfolio. Two patterns emerge. First, the U.S. equity/gold portfolio showed a higher historical median return than the U.S. equity/U.S. bond portfolio across all investment horizons. Second, the two portfolios exhibit different return profiles over time. At the 1-year horizon, both portfolios display similar fat-tailed distributions and negative skewness. However, as the holding period lengthens, their return distributions evolve differently. By the 10-year horizon, the return distribution of the U.S. equity/gold portfolio becomes close to symmetric, whereas the U.S. equity/U.S. bond portfolio continues to exhibit a degree of downside skewness. The results suggest the equity/gold portfolio historically delivered higher median returns and fewer extreme negative longer-term outcomes than the equity/bond portfolio. As shown in the 10-year panel of Chart 5 , the equity/gold portfolio earned a positive annualized return in every rolling 10-year period examined across the 30-year sample. Its weakest 10-year outcomes were also better than those of the equity/bond portfolio. Chart 5: Equity/gold returns were more symmetrically distributed at the 10-year holding horizon Image Periods of market stress provide another useful test of how bonds and gold behave as diversifiers. To keep the comparison consistent, we continue to focus on the same two portfolios: a 50% U.S. equity / 50% U.S. bond portfolio and a 50% U.S. equity / 50% gold portfolio and examine how these portfolios performed using three drawdown measures: maximum drawdown (the peak-to-trough loss), drawdown duration (the time taken to reach the trough), and recovery duration (the time needed to recover from the trough to the previous peak). Chart 6: Equity blended with bonds or gold softened losses or shortened recoveries across most crises Image As shown in Chart 6 , adding either U.S. bonds or gold to a U.S. equity portfolio generally improved portfolio resilience across the four crisis periods examined, both by reducing maximum drawdowns and shortening recovery periods. During the Dotcom Crash, GFC, and COVID Crisis, both diversified portfolios experienced materially smaller maximum drawdowns than the 100% equity portfolio, with the U.S. Equity/U.S. Bond Portfolio providing slightly greater downside protection than the U.S. Equity/Gold Portfolio in all three episodes. The Inflation Shock displayed a markedly different pattern for bonds. The U.S. equity/U.S. bond Portfolio declined by 34.1%, nearly matching the 35.0% drawdown of the 100% U.S. equity portfolio, suggesting that bonds provided little downside protection during this episode. By comparison, the U.S. equity/gold Portfolio experienced a smaller drawdown of 23.7%, indicating that gold's diversification characteristics remained broadly consistent with those observed in previous crisis periods. The recovery duration was equally telling: the U.S. equity/U.S. bond Portfolio required 2.8 years to recover, significantly longer than the 1.2 years required by the 100% U.S. equity portfolio. By contrast, the U.S. Equity/Gold Portfolio recovered in just 0.7 years, about six months earlier than the pure equity portfolio. Overall, both bonds and gold provided meaningful diversification benefits across most crisis periods by reducing drawdowns and improving recovery outcomes. The Inflation Shock, however, stood out as a notable exception for bonds, with limited downside protection and a substantially longer recovery period, which reinforces the earlier observation that the diversification benefit of bonds weakened during the Inflationary Reset regime. Conclusion Adding either bonds or gold to equities provided diversification benefits in the historical analysis, as reflected in the Diversification Ratio and crisis-period outcomes. Bonds generally produced higher DRs, with the greatest benefit during the GFC and weaker results when inflation and rising interest rates pressured both equities and bonds. Gold produced lower but steadier DRs. The equity/gold portfolio also recorded higher median returns and fewer extreme negative outcomes over longer holding periods, while providing more consistent drawdown protection across the crises examined. title: Chartstopper: September 25, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: It’s been a rollercoaster ride of a week for markets.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Nasdaq-100® hits record high, ends week up 3% 10-year yields jump to 5.15%, highest since 2007 Strong PMI and hawkish Fed comments lift hike odds Oil swings on mixed Iran diplomacy signals Meta's Muse agent boosts AI trade momentum This Week Positive sentiment to start the week initially pushed Treasury yields lower and the Nasdaq-100® to a record high, but that all changed on Wednesday. The week started off strong, with the early success of Meta’s new Muse agent boosting the artificial intelligence (AI) trade . Plus, U.S. oil prices fell $10 from last Friday to $90 per barrel as Saudi Arabia prepared to reopen its East-West pipeline and President Trump said the U.S. and Iran had “ very good ” talks and another meeting was scheduled “in the very near future.” Then on Wednesday, 10-year Treasury yields rose 15 basis points (bp) in a day on fears the Federal Reserve will have to hikes rate more than expected because: The economy looks surprisingly strong, with the preliminary September S&P PMI unexpectedly rising to a five-year high and broad-based strength in new orders and employment for Manufacturing and Services. Fed Governor Michael Barr said his “base case” is for multiple rate hikes , after last week’s median Fed projection showed just one more hike , pushing up October rate hike odds about 65% from 55%. Hopes for a diplomatic resolution with Iran faded after Iran’s president spoke at the United Nations General Assembly, saying no meaningful negotiations can take place until the U.S. naval blockade ends and Iranian assets are unfrozen, helping push U.S. oil prices back above $95 . Reports yesterday that the U.S. and Iran are discussing a “ phased deal ” to reopen of the Strait of Hormuz helped lower oil prices a bit, but didn’t stop the run up in bond yields. So, with concerns about rate hikes rising, 10-year Treasury yields are up about 15bp this week to 5.15%, around their high since 2007. Despite this, the Nasdaq-100® is up 3% for the week, just below Tuesday’s record high. title: Climate Week NYC: How Five Companies are Advancing the Energy Transition
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Climate Week NYC brought private and public-sector leaders to New York this week to share progress on sustainability goals. Nasdaq marked the occasion by hosting the Dynamo Energy Transition Summit.
content: Climate Week NYC brought private and public-sector leaders to New York this week to share progress on sustainability goals. Nasdaq marked the occasion by hosting the Dynamo Energy Transition Summit on Sept. 22 at MarketSite, convening senior leaders across energy, technology, finance, and policy to examine the capital, innovation, and infrastructure driving the next phase of the global energy transition. Across the week, five companies detailed work that is moving decarbonization from commitment to construction. The consistent theme: the technologies needed to meet rising electricity demand while cutting emissions are being built now, not promised for later. Here's a look at how five companies are addressing these rising energy demands and decarbonization goals using innovative technology: TerraPower: Nuclear Optimized for the 21st-Century Grid Electricity demand is surging at a pace the current grid was not built for, driven by data centers, electrification, and industrial growth. TerraPower is engineering nuclear energy into a safer, faster, and more flexible form of zero-carbon power. Its Natrium plants pair an advanced nuclear reactor with a molten salt energy storage system that can boost output from 345MW to 500MW on demand, allowing the facility to respond to demand spikes during extreme weather or when renewable generation dips. The Natrium plant, already under construction in Wyoming, is on track to become the first utility-scale advanced nuclear power plant in the U.S. In January 2026, Meta signed an agreement with TerraPower to fund up to eight Natrium units by 2035. "TerraPower is proving that reliable, zero-carbon power at scale isn't a future bet, it's an energy solution ready to build today," said Chris Levesque, President and CEO of TerraPower. Rehlko: Speed and Sustainability Without the Trade-Off Image As demand for AI-driven data centers accelerates, operators must balance speed to power with asset longevity without increasing environmental impact. Rehlko's Structured Transition Model integrates backup and prime power technologies into a single framework, combining battery storage, microgrids, maintenance services, and lower-carbon fuels. The approach lets market participants meet urgent power demands while improving efficiency and sustainability. Rehlko extends the model through its Power Impact Intelligence platform, which evaluates the carbon impact of power systems, and programs like Conscious Care™, which reduce fuel consumption, operating hours, and emissions without compromising reliability. According to its 2026 Powering Impact Report, Rehlko has cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 19.6% since its 2023 baseline through energy efficiency investment and lower-carbon fuel adoption. "The rapid growth of AI and digital infrastructure requires a new approach to power," said Brian Melka, President and CEO of Rehlko. "At Rehlko, we're helping customers secure reliable power faster while advancing efficiency, resilience, and sustainability across the energy ecosystem." "As energy demand continues to grow, we believe reliability, efficiency, and sustainability can reinforce one another," said Francis Perrin, Chief Brand and Sustainability Officer at Rehlko. Perrin further states, "our focus is on helping customers make informed decisions that create long-term value while supporting their climate and resilience goals." Helion: Fusion as Practical, Always-On Power Image Meeting global climate goals will require far more carbon-free electricity than the grid can provide today. Helion is working to make fusion a practical source of reliable, always-on power that can meet rising energy demand without producing carbon emissions. Fusion fuel is widely available, and the technology can provide consistent power regardless of weather, complementing other clean energy sources. Helion is now building Orion, its first commercial fusion power plant, in Malaga, Washington. Orion is designed to deliver at least 50 megawatts of electricity to the grid. "Bringing fusion electricity to the grid at meaningful commercial power levels is an important step toward a future where clean, safe, and reliable energy is abundantly available to help address our climate goals," said David Kirtley, CEO of Helion. Hudson Technologies: Reclaiming Refrigerant to Cut Virgin Demand Refrigerants are ubiquitous and rarely noticed, present in building cooling systems, vehicles, and industrial equipment. They are also a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions when mishandled. Hudson Technologies services those systems, recovering refrigerant, purifying it, and returning it to the marketplace for reuse. The company was founded in 1991 and went public on Nasdaq in 1994. Founder Kevin Zugibe identified an opportunity in refrigerant recovery and reclamation using mobile equipment, an approach refined after Hudson was called to Ground Zero to remove refrigerant from systems below the World Trade Center site. The company has since expanded from chiller servicing into data centers and residential servicing, growing its services business alongside pure refrigerant recovery and resale. Keeping chillers running efficiently also controls energy costs, since inefficient units consume substantially more power. Ken Gaglione, Chairman, President, and CEO of Hudson Technologies, described the company's mission: "That reuse and recycle is our commitment. That's our mission at Hudson — to reduce the amount of virgin refrigerant that's necessary and thereby impact global warming." Plug Power: Hydrogen Built Around What Market Participants Need Plug Power built its hydrogen business by listening to customers to figure out what would be needed to make hydrogen a big part of the energy transition and the energy economy. “We listened to customers like Walmart and they told us in the logistics environment that using batteries in forklifts in their distribution centers was a source of loss of productivity. So, what we discovered is that transition to a clean technology just by itself and just because of decarbonization is not enough. You need to bring something else — more value to your customers.” said Jose Luis Crespo, CEO of Plug Power. The company now has more than 70,000 forklifts running on fuel cells across the U.S. and Europe with companies including Walmart, Amazon, BMW, and Home Depot. Plug Power considers this the first commercial application for hydrogen fuel cells, demonstrating that decarbonization can deliver competitive advantage alongside emissions reductions. “I think that's the key, and I think that's what convinced us that hydrogen could play a big role and will play a big role in the energy transition.” Information is provided by the companies and is for educational purposes only. title: Smart Routers Already Trade Through Lit Orders
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: Routers don't always hit the best-priced liquidity. In fact, SEC data reveals frequent trade-throughs of odd lots.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Odd Lots Often Ignored: Up to 10% of 1-share trades and 20% of dark pool trades trade through better-priced odd lots. Partial Fills Worsen the Picture: Including partial-fill opportunities raises the trade-through rate by ~60%. After-Hours Gaps Widen: Pre-market trade-throughs 67% higher and post-market 33% higher than regular hours — same rules, different behavior. Visibility ≠ Execution: Routers don't always hit better-priced lit liquidity, undermining the core case for rescinding OPR. Since Reg NMS was adopted back in 2005, U.S. equity markets have become much more automated and efficient. A core premise of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) proposal to rescind Order Protection Rule (OPR) is that modern routers will take the best priced liquidity regardless of whether OPR exists or not. But when we look at how routing actually performs (even with OPR), the data gives us pause. Odd-lot quotes have always been there, but sometimes get ignored We know that odd lots are not protected, but they have always been on data feeds . And this academic study showed that the odd-lot midpoint was often very different from the National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO) midpoint (in a way that informed traders about market direction), so they’re also important liquidity for traders. Following the logic above, if a router really does go where the liquidity is, then we should never see trade-throughs of odd lots. Interestingly, the SEC’s own analysis in its rule proposal says otherwise. Chart 1: Off-exchange trades tend to trade through odd lots more than on-exchange trades Image In fact, the SEC data (above) shows that: Up to 10% of 1-share trades on the tape traded through a better priced odd-lot order. Even larger orders (like 20-share orders) traded through odd lots that would fill the order at better prices. Dark pools ignore lit odd lots even more — as much as 20% of the time. Interestingly, an academic who filed a comment letter on the OPR proposal argues that the situation is even worse than it appears. That’s because the SEC data only counts a trade-through as such if the entire order could have gotten the better price. But what if a 15-share order could have hit a 7-share order at a better price? If you include them, the academic estimates that the trade-through rate increases by 60%. Chart 2: Including potential partial fills push the trade-through rate higher Image What about trade-throughs after hours? Another way to see if routers are rational or not is to look at how the market changes after hours. Many exchanges still publish firm quotes in the after-hours markets, and that still includes odd lots. But the SEC’s data again shows that the trade-through rate outside regular hours is noticeably higher than that during regular hours: Pre-market odd lots are 67% more likely to be traded through than during regular hours. Meanwhile, post-market trade-through rate is 33% higher than during regular market hours. Chart 3: Trade-through rate is higher outside regular hours Image Sure, odd lots aren’t protected, and data shows routers sometimes ignore them The debate here isn’t whether it matters if odd lots are protected (we looked at that recently ). It is whether routers are profit maximizing enough to take all the better priced liquidity because they can still see it. These results, from the SEC’s own proposal, show routers don’t always trade with advertised liquidity at better prices – even if that would only partially fill the order. We also see that routing behavior changes outside regular hours, even though the rules for routing to odd lots don’t change.

title: From Monolith to Modular: How CSDs Are Rethinking Infrastructure for Changing Markets
author: Gerard Smith
description: The ongoing evolution of markets is forcing change to infrastructure. How are CSDs architecting for modern markets?
content: Key Takeaways CSDs are moving from monolithic platforms toward modular architectures that can adapt more easily to market and regulatory change. Cloud and containerized deployment can support resilience and scalability, but adoption must account for jurisdictional and supervisory constraints. Data architecture is becoming core operational infrastructure as CSDs manage broader asset types, counterparties and reporting demands. Digital assets and AI create new opportunities, but both require strong governance, auditability, legal certainty and institutional coordination.

title: Why Global Capital Is Betting on Texas
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq Texas convened ConnecTXions, a gathering of bankers, asset managers, infrastructure executives, and policymakers shaping the Texas economy.
content: 10 takeaways from Nasdaq Texas ConnecTXions in Dallas On Friday, September 18 in Dallas, Nasdaq Texas convened ConnecTXions, a gathering of bankers, asset managers, infrastructure executives, and policymakers shaping the Texas economy. The premise, as Nasdaq Texas President Rachel Racz framed it beforehand, is that the lines between public and private markets are blurring, capital allocators have more choices than ever, and companies are competing for investor attention across a more complex ecosystem. That backdrop set the day’s central themes: where capital is flowing, why Texas keeps attracting it, how companies compete for it, and what role public markets play in the next phase of growth. The day opened with a fireside chat between President George W. Bush and Racz on leadership and decision-making. "Decisions based upon principles are enduring," Bush told the room, a line that carried through to the two panels that followed. The conversations examined the mechanics of an evolving capital markets ecosystem. Here is what stood out: Trends in Asset Allocation and How Texas Plays a Role In the first panel of the day, Nasdaq's Yanni Angelakos, Head of CAP Investment Insights, sat down with Rich Nuzum, Head of OCIO, Franklin Templeton, and Michael Lane, EVP and Head of Asset Management, SEI, to unpack where institutional investors and wealth management capital is actually being deployed, and why Texas keeps showing up in the conversation. Portfolio construction is being redefined. Lane argued that goal-based investing should drive allocation decisions. "What is the money for?" he asked. In addition, stock and bond returns continue to show positive correlations. It may be more appropriate to reframe the traditional "60 (public market equities)/40 (public market fixed income)" portfolio to, instead, "60% public markets, 40% private markets," reflecting more holistic portfolios and a search for true ballast. Texas's scale lets capital go deep. Nuzum put it plainly: "If you want to go deep somewhere, Texas is the place to do it." If Texas were its own nation, it would rank among the world's largest economies, large enough for specialized investors to build focused, meaningful exposure. "Texas is big enough to matter globally. It moves the needle for portfolio allocation, and yet it's focused," he said. Texas is a live test of the AI investment thesis. Nuzum called the state "a microcosm" of whether the broader economy can deliver on the productivity promise of digitalization, pointing to the convergence of power generation, data centers, and compute demand within its borders. The wealth channel has an education gap. Individual investors and their advisors are still catching up to how private markets behave differently from public ones, particularly around liquidity, and to the importance of balancing both within an asset allocation framework, Lane noted. Texas has become a global case study. Viewing Texas as a model for economic competitiveness, Finance ministers and state treasurers from other countries now ask Nuzum how to replicate what Texas has built. "These days, I point them to Texas," he said. What’s Behind “Texas’s Edge”? If the first conversation followed where capital is flowing, the second explained why so much of it is landing in Texas. Racz moderated a discussion with Ned Fleming of SunTx and Jeremy Ford of Hilltop Holdings on the infrastructure, financing, and policy choices fueling the state's growth. Framing the discussion, Racz asked, "What makes Texas the place where you want to keep building?” Both executives were candid about what could slow the momentum, from affordability to political durability, but their message was ultimately a call to stay engaged with the people building Texas's economy, not just the capital flowing into it. Three pillars supporting Texas’ growth. Fleming described Texas's advantage as people, pro-business government, and sustained infrastructure investment working together. "When you build infrastructure and you finish infrastructure, it allows people to come," he said, citing a single Frisco interchange that catalyzed $50 billion in nearby investment. The numbers underscore Texas’ edge. Texas has invested $20 billion in infrastructure, more than North Carolina, South Carolina, Alabama, and Tennessee combined, while state GDP has grown from roughly $750 billion to $3 trillion over 25 years. Financing is keeping pace with growth. Ford noted that Hilltop's municipal advisory business had a record year, with commercial construction and development lending up double-digit percentages year over year – reflecting Hilltop’s broader activity, including its significant Texas business. Growth is statewide, not just Dallas and Austin. Ford pointed to real momentum in the Rio Grande Valley and the Permian Basin as evidence that Texas's growth is not confined to its largest metros. The risks ahead are political and social, not economic. Both panelists flagged affordability and the need for wage growth to keep pace with GDP growth. As Fleming put it: "People matter. Don't forget the people matter at every single level of an organization." The Nasdaq Texas Thread Across both panels and the fireside chat, one message was clear: Texas's economic momentum is not accidental. It reflects decades of deliberate choices around tax policy, regulation, infrastructure investment, and a business court system designed to compete with Delaware. Together, those factors have helped transform Texas from a regional success story into a market that global capital allocators increasingly view as impossible to ignore. As Racz put it from the stage, "Nasdaq Texas enables the connections that power the state's economy." Learn more about Nasdaq Texas.

title: Treasury hits Russia's VTB Bank with new sanctions over Iran ties
description: The new Russian bank sanctions follow a small handful of other actions that the Trump administration has taken since vowing to inflict "economic D-Day" on Iran.
content: A photo shows an exterior view of a branch of Russia's VTB Bank, on May 23, 2023 in Tehran, Iran. Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu Agency | Getty Images The Treasury Department on Monday announced new sanctions on Russia's state-controlled VTB Bank as part of its effort to economically isolate Iran by targeting its business partners and other financial "enablers." The action, which followed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's promise that a "large bank" would be sanctioned on Monday, was the latest penalty to be doled out as part of "Operation Economic Outcast," the Trump administration's non-military warfare strategy against Iran. The new sanctions against VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company, Russia's second-largest bank, stemmed from allegations that it helped Tehran evade sanctions in part by "establishing correspondent relationships with sanctioned Iranian banks." The new financial action, which Treasury expects to block at least tens of millions of dollars, makes VTB "among the most comprehensively sanctioned financial institutions in the world," Treasury said in a press release . That's because the bank was already sanctioned by the U.S. in 2022 and early 2025 under the Biden administration. But curbing the bank may indirectly lead to economic limits on China, which is the top buyer of Iran's oil. Some observers were quick to raise questions about how much of an impact the new sanctions would have. "We're still digesting it a little bit," Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research, told CNBC following Treasury's announcement. While VTB is a large bank in Russia, it has already been significantly sanctioned, Marcus noted. "The devil does tend to be in the details," he said. "Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise," Bessent said in a statement. "Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers." Monday's action follows a small handful of other sanctions the Trump administration has imposed since last month, when it vowed to unleash "economic D-Day" on Iran and hobble its regime through global economic pressure. VTB is reportedly the only Russian bank with a branch in China. "This is a China play," Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and former U.S. Treasury sanctions official, said in an X post. "What changes today: every Chinese bank touching VTB Shanghai now carries Iran-program secondary-sanctions exposure, inside an operation where Treasury is naming a bank a week," Maleki wrote. "Beijing has shielded its big banks from the Russia fight. Shielding them from the Iran fight is a different calculation," he wrote, noting Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to meet with President Donald Trump later this month. title: Counting the votes: Warsh faces a tough battle as the Fed girds for expected interest rate hike
description: Traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase, as well as a more than 75% chance for another one in December.
content: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty Images Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh faces a tricky head count this week when he and his fellow policymakers decide on both the immediate and future path of interest rates. While markets have honed in on a near-certain quarter percentage point hike in Wednesday's vote, it's not at all clear how broad will be the margin among the 12 Federal Open Market Committee voters. Moreover, Warsh will have to decide how to message the move: Will this be the rare one-and-done on hikes, will there be more to come or will the chair maintain his cryptic posture in not trying to guide markets one way or the other? "With the market priced this way, it would be shocking if he came in and did nothing," Bill Dudley, the former New York Fed president, said in a CNBC interview. "It would really damage his credibility because it would basically be all talk, no action." Indeed, as of Monday afternoon, futures traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase this week, as well as a more than 75% chance that the FOMC would follow up in December with another move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Fed funds, the benchmark overnight borrowing rate, currently stand at 3.50% to 3.75%. The greater probabilities follow another run-up in fuel prices and inflation data last wee k that showed prices continued to climb in August. Both trends followed Warsh's comments a few weeks ago that the Fed would be forced into action unless there are more concrete signs that inflation is easing back to the central bank's 2% target. However, there are substantial complications. Wait or act? For one thing, the Fed historically has looked through the type of trends that are fueling inflation now. Economists generally agree that much of this year's increase has come from tariffs and an energy supply shock from the Iran war, both of which have uncertain impacts on the long-range trajectory of inflation. "We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate," Goldman Sachs economist David Mericle said in a client note. "We think that all of the overshoot of 2% can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade." Nevertheless, Goldman changed its call from no change at this week's meeting to a hike, primarily because the firm's economists think the market expectations will force the Fed to move. Whether that also will be the case on an FOMC that voted 9-3 in favor of a hold at the July meeting is another matter. The three dissenters — regional presidents Lorie Logan of Dallas, Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis — all supported a quarter-point hike two months ago, when the Fed last met. Assuming their positions haven't changed, and there's been nothing in their public comments to suggest they have, that would mean four other members would have to switch their votes from hold to hike. Arguably the most-watched voter is Governor Christopher Waller. In public remarks delivered Sept. 3, Waller voiced suppor t for another hold at this meeting, albeit with the usual caveats about watching data to confirm that disinflation trends are continuing. Mostly, he merely urged patience rather than a rush to hike. "What's the cost of waiting one meeting? Hiking 25 basis points, one meeting right now, is not going to bring the [consumer price index] down to 2%," he said. The CPI for August actually showed headline inflation running at a 3.4% rate, though the core rate, which excludes food and soaring energy costs, was a more benign 2.4%, down 0.1 percentage point from July. Waller wasn't alone in advocating patience — New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC less than two weeks ago that a "wait-and-see" approach seems to make sense. Earlier in the summer, Williams, whose perch atop the New York Fed is traditionally considered part of the influential "troika" of influence at the central bank, said he thinks inflation has peaked . Also in recent remarks, Governor Michael Barr expressed concern about temporary inflation taking deeper hold and said he would be open to a hike, not set on one. The FOMC breakdown So who would join the three July dissenters? Warsh is largely expected to be part of the hiking group, considering his remarks in Jackson Hole, Wyoming last month. Governor Lisa Cook said in early August that she's "prepared to act" to take on inflation. Conversely, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson and Chicago's Austan Goolsbee also have counseled a more patient approach. That would leave Governors Philip Jefferson, who is the vice chair; Jerome Powell , the former chair, who has kept a decidedly low profile since stepping down from the top spot, and Michelle Bowman, who spoke little on monetary policy over the summer and whose last related remarks were in May, when she also expressed concern about hiking unnecessarily. Then there's a larger wildcard: Should Warsh press the case for a hike, would those on the fence simply cross over to his side in the interest of presenting a united front? The vote margin not only will reveal the extent of the intellectual divide on the committee between those who think inflation is temporary and those who believe price pressures are becoming entrenched. It also will provide important signals about how effectively Warsh's leadership is reverberating inside the Fed. "It should be noted that, if the Fed does indeed raise rates this week, it may not look, in retrospect, like a close call," David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said in his weekly market note. "If a majority within the committee coalesces around a decision to hike, the other members may well join them to portray a more united front to the public and the President." In such a case, Kelly said the final vote could see two, one or no dissents. From there, markets will look at the Fed's "dot plot" update. The grid spells out, anonymously, the rate expectations for the full 19 participants at the meeting, though Warsh withheld his dot for the June update. Investors will look for how much conviction there will be for two hikes this year, as well as the outlook for 2027. This will also feature the first look at 2029. The Fed almost never hikes or cuts just once but rather moves in cycles, as policymakers view incremental one-off moves as ineffective. A 10-8 split in favor of one hike — assuming Warsh's disdain for forward guidance and nonparticipation in the update — would indicate that "some participants might be ambivalent about the first hike and some might want to avoid pushing market expectations any higher," Mericle wrote. "But we see a risk of a majority for two hikes if more participants than we expect see a hike this week as a normal response to higher oil prices and AI demand and the start of a series of rate hikes," he added. In the case of a close divide on the committee, attention then will turn to Warsh's news conference Wednesday afternoon, and how the chair conveys FOMC sentiment. Dudley, the former New York Fed chief, said "the Fed needs to explain how they're thinking about the economy." "Now [Warsh has] just got to follow that up with action," Dudley said. "If he does that, I think he's basically fixed the problem that he created in his first two press conferences."
